data.command: Explain T1583 Acquire Infrastructure resource development

data.text:
# T1583: Acquire Infrastructure

**Tactic:** Resource Development (TA0042)
**Type:** Pre-compromise technique

## Overview

T1583 describes adversaries **buying, leasing, renting, or otherwise legitimately obtaining** infrastructure that will later support their operations. Because this activity happens before any contact with the victim environment — and often through legitimate commercial providers — it's largely invisible to the target until the infrastructure is weaponized.

This contrasts with **T1584 (Compromise Infrastructure)**, where adversaries take over third-party systems they don't own. T1583 is about *lawful acquisition* (even if paid for with stolen cards or fake identities), which makes it harder to disrupt through takedowns and harder to attribute.

## Sub-techniques

| ID | Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| T1583.001 | **Domains** | Registering domains for phishing, C2, watering holes, or typosquatting |
| T1583.002 | **DNS Server** | Running authoritative DNS to control resolution for C2 domains |
| T1583.003 | **Virtual Private Server** | Renting VPS instances for C2 servers, redirectors, exfil staging |
| T1583.004 | **Server** | Physical/dedicated servers, often from bulletproof hosting providers |
| T1583.005 | **Botnet** | Renting access to existing botnets for spam, DDoS, or proxying |
| T1583.006 | **Web Services** | Abusing legitimate platforms (cloud storage, code repos, social media APIs) as dead drops or C2 channels |
| T1583.007 | **Serverless** | Using Lambda/Functions/Workers as redirectors or C2 endpoints to blend with cloud traffic |
| T1583.008 | **Malvertising** | Purchasing legitimate ad inventory to deliver malicious content |

## Why Adversaries Do This

- **Anonymity layering** — cryptocurrency payments, stolen credit cards, fake registrant identities, privacy-protected WHOIS
- **Resilience** — fast-flux DNS, multiple redundant C2 nodes, disposable domains
- **Evasion** — infrastructure hosted in the victim's own country/cloud region blends with normal traffic; serverless and CDN fronting hide true origins
- **Separation of roles** — distinct infrastructure for recon, delivery, C2, and exfiltration so one takedown doesn't kill the operation

## Common Patterns

- Domains registered weeks-to-months before use ("aging" to bypass new-domain filters)
- Bulletproof hosting providers in jurisdictions with weak abuse handling
- Reseller accounts to add an extra ownership hop
- Domain fronting through CDNs
- LetsEncrypt-style free TLS certificates to look legitimate

## Detection (Post-compromise visibility)

Since acquisition is pre-compromise, detection focuses on the **usage signature**:

- **Certificate Transparency log monitoring** — catch lookalike domains the moment a cert is issued
- **Passive DNS + newly observed domain (NOD) feeds** — flag fresh domains resolving to your org's brand terms
- **Homoglyph/typosquat detection** on inbound email and web traffic
- **Infrastructure overlap analysis** — shared TLS certs, registrant emails, netblocks, and nameservers linking campaigns
- **Threat intel** on known bulletproof hosters and adversary-preferred VPS providers
- Egress filtering alerting on traffic to low-reputation or recently registered domains

## Mitigation Reality Check

MITRE classifies this as occurring outside the victim's defensive boundary, so traditional mitigations barely apply. Effective countermeasures are mostly **ecosystem-level**: registrar/hosting provider abuse processes, takedown coordination, and defensive blocking (domain reputation, NOD blocking in proxies and secure email gateways).

Want me to go deeper on any sub-technique — e.g., how serverless C2 redirectors work, or how to build CT-log monitoring for lookalike domains?
